title: Zoute Grand Prix 2026
excerpt: A city-scale celebration where supercars, classics and concours machinery spill far beyond the official venues.

sections.heading: A City Taken Over
sections.text:
At most automotive events, there is a clear moment when you arrive.

A gate. A ticket. A lawn. A circuit.

At Zoute Grand Prix, that line is much harder to find.

By the time we arrived in Knokke on Sunday afternoon, the event seemed to have escaped whatever boundaries had been created for it. BMW M cars mixed with Porsches, Lamborghinis and Ferraris in the streets. Something interesting could appear at a junction, outside a hotel, along the seafront or simply in traffic.

After a while, spotting another remarkable car almost became a game.

Turn one corner and there might be nothing.

Turn the next and there could be something you had been hoping to see all year.

That scale is deliberate. For 2026, Zoute Grand Prix Car Week ran from 7 to 11 October across several areas of Knokke-Heist rather than one central venue, with rallies, auctions, new-car displays, the Concours d’Élégance and other activities happening simultaneously across the town.

It made the afternoon feel less like visiting an event and more like arriving in a city that had temporarily changed its priorities.

For a few days, cars came first.

sections.heading: The Kinder Surprise Effect
sections.text:
That may have been the most addictive part of Zoute.

You never really knew what would appear next.

There were so many Porsches, Ferraris, Lamborghinis and BMW M cars around Knokke that eventually even machines that would draw a crowd almost anywhere else began to feel strangely normal.

And then something genuinely unexpected would appear and reset the scale again.

It is difficult to reproduce that feeling at a conventional concours. At Chantilly or Hampton Court, you know where the cars will be. At London Concours, the walls of the Honourable Artillery Company define the experience.

At Zoute, the possibility extends beyond the official displays.

You keep walking because the next street might contain something better than the last.

Our single afternoon inevitably meant missing part of that spectacle. Cars such as the Koenigseggs and Bugatti Chiron Super Sport that had been circulating during the week escaped us entirely.

But strangely, that almost reinforces the point.

You cannot really “complete” Zoute in a few hours.

There is always another part of Knokke you did not walk through, another arrival you missed or another car that appeared ten minutes after you left.

sections.heading: A Different Kind of Concours
sections.text:
The Green Grounds offered a very different experience.

For 2026, the Zoute Concours d’Élégance returned after several years away, with selected pre- and post-war cars competing across the golf-course setting on Saturday and Sunday.

For someone primarily drawn towards contemporary supercars, however, the contrast with the streets was noticeable.

The concours leaned heavily into historic machinery. There was plenty to appreciate — craftsmanship, provenance and cars that rarely appear outside collections — but after the almost uncontrolled variety found around Knokke, the modern performance selection on the golf course felt comparatively restrained.

Two cars changed that.

An Aston Martin Valkyrie AMR Pro and Ferrari 849 Testarossa, positioned beside one another, created one of the strongest visual pairings of the afternoon.

They could hardly approach performance in more different ways.

The AMR Pro is the track-only extreme of the Valkyrie programme: its wheelbase is 380 mm longer than the road car’s, its aerodynamics generate roughly twice the downforce, and its Cosworth-built 6.5-litre naturally aspirated V12 revs to 11,000 rpm and develops around 1,000 bhp. It was developed free from both road-homologation requirements and racing regulations.

Beside it sat something considerably newer.

sections.heading: Two Extremes, Side by Side
sections.text:
Ferrari unveiled the 849 Testarossa only in September 2025 as the replacement for the SF90 Stradale.

Its return of the Testarossa name connects the car to a designation Ferrari first used in the 1950s for racing engines with red-painted cam covers, before it became synonymous with the famous 1980s road car. Underneath the historical name, though, the new 849 is thoroughly contemporary: a plug-in hybrid combining an 830 cv twin-turbocharged V8 with three electric motors for a total output of 1,050 cv.

Seeing it next to the Valkyrie AMR Pro worked precisely because the cars were so different.

The Aston looks almost devoid of anything unnecessary, all tunnels, surfaces and aero developed around track performance.

The Ferrari remains recognisably a road car, extreme, but still conceived to combine its performance with the usability expected from a modern Ferrari flagship.

On a concours lawn otherwise dominated by history, the pair offered a brief glimpse of two very different ideas of what automotive excess looks like today.

And personally, it was difficult not to wish there had been a little more of it.

After events such as London Concours, where an entire lawn could be consumed by modern hypercars, Zoute’s contemporary selection on the Green Grounds felt smaller than expected.

The cars that were there were exceptional.

We simply wanted more of them.

sections.heading: Exclusive in More Ways Than One
sections.text:
Zoute also made its exclusivity unusually visible.

There were people experiencing the event entirely through the public streets and displays.

Others had day tickets.

Beyond that were additional areas, hospitality spaces and venues requiring their own level of access.

The 2026 programme itself was built around distinct zones: the Gallery by EY, the Green Grounds, the Marquee by Bonhams and the new 4x4 Village in Heist, alongside freely accessible displays on the Car Boulevard.

There is an obvious logic to that structure. Zoute combines an enormous public audience with collectors, manufacturers, auction houses, rally participants and hospitality guests, all occupying the town at the same time.

But from our perspective, it also created an interesting contradiction.

At Chantilly, the environment appeared more formally elegant, dress codes, hats, the château, the Garden Party, yet once inside, the experience felt remarkably inclusive.

Zoute was almost the reverse.

The streets were casual and open, but some of the most interesting parts of the event existed behind increasingly specific layers of access.

That does not erase the spectacle.

It simply changes how you experience it.

You can feel completely surrounded by Zoute Grand Prix while simultaneously knowing that you are seeing only one part of it.

sections.heading: When Knokke Becomes the Parade
sections.text:
By late afternoon, the city-scale nature of Zoute made sense again.

Sunday was also the final day of the Zoute GT Tour, a programme dedicated to modern and youngtimer GT cars. Cars had left Knokke earlier in the morning, with the official schedule bringing them back through the event later that afternoon before the final arrival at the Gallery between 5 and 7 p.m.

That return was when the streets became the spectacle again.

Cars appeared in motion rather than perfectly arranged on lawns. Engines echoed between buildings. Crowds collected along the routes and the distinction between participant, visitor and ordinary Knokke traffic became temporarily blurred.

Those were probably the moments that best explained why Zoute feels different from the other events we attended in 2026.

It is not simply the Concours.

It is not the Gallery.

It is not one rally or one collection.

It is the cumulative effect of all of them occupying the same town.

You can spend an afternoon walking through Knokke and still leave knowing that you missed entire sections of the event.

That can be frustrating.

It is also part of the appeal.

Because during Zoute Grand Prix, the next remarkable car is rarely confined to a stand.

Sometimes it is simply waiting around the next corner.
